newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Former Yugoslav foes cut arms, but problems remain.
newsitem.headline: Former Yugoslav foes cut arms, but problems remain.

text.p: The Bosnian Serbs are beginning to reduce their arsenals in line with a regional arms control pact, after dragging their feet, but problems remain to be ironed out, a senior Western arms negotiator said on Friday.

Norwegian general Vigleik Eide of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) was in Vienna to review the progress of arms cuts agreed to last year by the Bosnian Serbs, the Moslem-Croat Federation, Croatia and Yugoslavia.

"As long as it is not done, I regard all the parties as a potential problem, and there are still questions around implementation, but it is encouraging that they are coming forward with detailed plans for continued reductions," he told a news conference.
The OSCE has been charged with overseeing a U.S.-backed arms control deal, signed in Florence last June, which commits the four parties to cutting their military hardware.
The deal is part of the U.S.-brokered Dayton peace package which ended 43 months of war in the region.
In the first phase of the reduction plan over 1,700 pieces from all four parties were destroyed, although the Bosnian Serbs only cut their arms by one tenth, Eide said.
The second phase, due to end in October, aims to destroy over 3,700 pieces of artillery, tanks and armoured vehicles.

Eide said Croatia had already completed its reduction, six months ahead of schedule. Yugoslavia had started its programme through permitted exports of arms but the bulk was due to begin in July and end in September, one month early.
"We have still a considerable amount of work to be done in Bosnia and Herzegovina," Eide noted.

The Bosnian Serbs had rattled the other parties by trying to use loopholes in the treaty to win exemptions, but in January they agreed to increase their reduction liability to over 1,000 pieces, Eide said.

"The Bosnian Serbs began their reduction two weeks ago and should be able to meet reductions, as they have defined them, by the end of the reduction period, with technical assistance from several countries," he said.

Squabbles about how to share out the reductions in the Moslem-Croat Federation had delayed their planning, but Eide was optimistic about their chances of meeting the target. The Federation starts work on the second phase in early June.

"There is no question that the technical capability exists for all parties to complete reductions by the deadline," he said. "But if you ask me to guarantee the parties will do this I cannot. It is up to them to keep their commitments."
